title: Adaptive KV Cache Lease Protocol — sketch
content:
Context / motivation:
- We currently have per-worker KV cache with soft TTL and on-miss fetch from a shared blob store.
- At high QPS with many short sessions, cache churn is high and duplicative fetches spike costs and tail latency.
- Need a lightweight coordination layer (lease/lock-ish) to reduce duplicate loads and allow workers to share ownership of hot prefixes without centralizing every access.

Goals:
- Prevent N concurrent workers from simultaneously fetching the same KV chunk during cache-miss storms.
- Keep latency SLOs: acquiring a short lease should be fast (<1ms local), fallbacks should be graceful.
- Avoid single point of contention. No heavyweight leader election for every key.
- Support adaptive lease duration depending on observed load and item hotness.
- Be compatible with private/dedicated/hosted deployments (should work for both in-process shared memory and multi-host via small coordination layer).

Design sketch (high-level):
- Each cache key can be in one of: "unowned", "leased", "shared".
- "Lease" = exclusive short-term right to fetch and populate the KV item and optionally serve it to others during the lease holder's fetch.
- Other workers encountering a miss will attempt to become a "waiter" for the key: they will either get the value from the lease-holder via peer RPC or fall back to remote fetch after timeout.

API shapes (minimal):
1) TryAcquireLease(key, local_node_id) -> {status: ok | busy, lease_id?, ttl_ms?}
- Ok: caller is lease-holder for ttl_ms.
- Busy: caller received info about current lease holder (holder_node_id) and optionally estimated remaining ttl_ms.

2) ReleaseLease(key, lease_id, optional: checksum) -> {status: released | not_found}
- Release is best-effort; expired leases auto-drop.

3) RenewLease(key, lease_id) -> {status: ok | denied, new_ttl_ms}
- Renewal allowed if holder still healthy; denied if lease already transferred.

4) ServeFromHolder(holder_node_id, key) (peer RPC): fetch value or stream during population.

5) ObserveHotness(key, sample: access_count, miss_count, avg_latency_ms) -> (used off-band by lease manager to tune TTLs)

Lease semantics (local optimistic-first):
- Prefer in-process fast path: try optimistic in-memory lease table (CAS) in worker. CAS success => holder. CAS fail => read holder info and become waiter.
- For multi-host, there's a tiny distributed lease store implemented on top of existing routing/consensus layer (e.g., small Raft per-shard or using consistent hash + gossip + soft-lease via signed tokens).
- Leases are intentionally short: base_ttl = 200ms, max_ttl adaptive up to 5s for extremely hot keys.
- When a lease is acquired, holder performs fetch and populates local cache and also streams to any waiters that registered.
- Waiters register a short-lived callback/ephemeral subscription to holder to receive data as soon as available (over existing peer RPC channel). If holder fails to respond within waiter_timeout (eg 150ms), waiters fallback to remote fetch and may attempt to become new lease-holder.

Adaptive TTL heuristics (rough idea):
- Every key has a small moving-window: hits per second (HPS), miss rate, average serve time.
- If HPS > threshold_hot && miss_rate low => extend TTL multiplicatively (x2) until max_ttl.
- If holder sees repeated renew failures or high queueing => shrink TTL to minimize holding lock under contention.
- Use exponential backoff for renew attempts when network failures observed.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Holder crash mid-fetch: lease expires naturally; waiters will fallback after waiter_timeout. To avoid double-fetch storm, staggered randomized retry with jitter and capped concurrency.
- Partition: in multi-host, two nodes may both think they hold lease due to clock skew; we prefer monotonic lease ids (epoch + node id + sequence) and require lease_id verification on release/renew.
- Long-tail stalls from too-long TTL: monitor renew latencies and reduce TTL if tail > SLO.

Metrics to emit (per-key aggregated / per-shard):
- lease_acquire_rate, lease_acquire_success_rate, avg_lease_ttl, lease_renew_failures, waiter_count_per_miss, average_waiter_latency, duplicate_fetch_suppression_rate.

Proto-ish examples (pseudocode):
- TryAcquireLease:
  let existing = lease_table.get(key)
  if existing == null {
    let new_lease = {id: make_lease_id(node_id), node: node_id, expires: now + base_ttl}
    if lease_table.cas(key, null, new_lease) success -> return ok,new_lease.id,base_ttl
    else -> return busy, lease_table.get(key)
  } else if existing.node == node_id {
    return ok, existing.id, existing.ttl
  } else {
    return busy, existing.node, existing.expires - now
  }
- Waiter flow (simplified):
  1) On miss, call TryAcquireLease
  2a) If ok: fetch from blobstore, populate, release or keep lease
  2b) If busy: register with holder (rpc RegisterWaiter(holder_node, key, my_node, cb_addr)) and sleep until cb or waiter_timeout
  3) If cb arrives with value -> populate and return
  4) If timeout -> attempt own TryAcquireLease (race) with jitter

Operational notes / implementation options:
- Single-process (edge) deployment: use shared memory hash table + futex/wakeup for waiters. Very low latency.
- Multi-host: options:
  * Small in-memory gossip/soft-lease: nodes advertise leases with signed tokens (no strict leader). Risk: split-brain for short durations but acceptable if TTL short and clients fallback.
  * Per-shard consensus (Raft) for strict correctness on small hot-shard set: heavier but predictable. Could be used only for very hot keys (auto-promote).
- Start with soft-lease design (gossip + signed tokens) and collect telemetry. If we see correctness issues for a small fraction of keys, implement per-shard strict leases for those keys.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What exact thresholds for hotness? (Need historical trace analysis across customer workloads) -> run SRV-2891 profiling job.
- Should we prioritize memory vs. network streaming for waiters? e.g., stream in chunks for large KV items.
- Integration with existing prefix/KV cache eviction policy and persistent store (leveldb/rocksdb) layout.
- Security: peer RPC auth when serving from holder (use mTLS + token from control plane).
- How to expose lease metrics to Redwood Console and per-tenant isolation? (tag metrics by tenant/model if possible)

Notes to self / next steps:
- Spike: implement single-host shared-memory flow + waiter futex approach (2-3 day spike).
- Add instrumentation: record duplicate-fetchs avoided per minute.
- Collect traces and synthetic test with N=50 concurrent misses to tune base_ttl and waiter_timeout.
- PR reference: start a branch runtime/kv-lease-spike and link to PR once minimal feature exists.

References / related tickets:
- GH: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/412 (lease token prototype, earlier idea)
- JIRA: SRV-2891 cache churn profiling job
- Slack: https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C01SERVING (thread: "kv lease idea")

Random sketchy ascii diagram (fast):
  [worker A] --TryAcquireLease(key)--> (local CAS success) --fetch--> [blobstore]
                     |
                     | register waiter via RPC
                     v
                [worker B] --TryAcquireLease--> busy -> RegisterWaiter -> wait for stream

End of sketch. TODO: make small executable prototype and run load test before writing API docs.
